utterances.text: As a professional forensic expert, is this photograph something you would take into account in establishing the number of bodies, for example, and establishing the cause of death and all the rest?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm guided as an expert exclusively by individual cases and analysis of each of these cases individually. So -- well, I'm not somebody who can assess that on a surface area you have such and such a number of people. If an expert who is able to analyse this superficial -- or rather, this photograph of this kind and then can tell you that his estimation was that there are 500 bodies on the photograph, where I have autopsy findings for 200 bodies, then I can only evaluate that through the number of bodies ascertained. But as a forensic expert, if you want me to discuss this, that's absolutely impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this connection let me ask you this: As a forensic expert, does it mean anything to you if, for example, a man would come and acknowledge that he had taken part in executions and said that there were more than a thousand people? Would that be a relevant piece of information for you to take this number and then take that as being the cause of death, the manner of death?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because it's not a fair question. In respect to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In respect to what? Someone comes over to the witness and says or the witness comes to know that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In respect to what, to a particular burial site?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you need to be specific. I mean, you can't be --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not talking of how many people were executed at any given time in any given place; we're talking about forensic examinations of recovered bodies. That's what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was subject of cross-examination. I'm strictly -- stick to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- just be more specific. Of course you can ask the question, but you need to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor on page 34, line 10, mentioned Erdemovic, Drazen Erdemovic, who testified here and who was convicted, as was stated, for having taken part in the execution of over a thousand men and who said how those people died. He asked you that within the same context that I'm putting your question to you. So my question to you within that context is should that have any bearing on your own work as a forensic pathologist with regards to the establishment of the number of people, the cause and manner of death, and so on?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I'll try and be brief in my answer and I'll answer in the same way that I answered the Prosecutor. All I'm interested in is facts, it's only facts that are valid for me to interpret them. Now, from the entire statement and testimony regardless of what the number is, the only relevant fact which I will retain in my head is that they were executed -- or rather, that they were hit by fire-arms, not to mention execution or anything. So from the whole statement the only thing that is relevant for me is the number if the number was mentioned by him and the way in which this was done. Now, through individual reports I will be able to see and provide proof and evidence to you on the basis of which you as the Trial Chamber will conclude whether his statement and testimony is valid or not. Do I make myself clear? The only valid thing for me is what I can see and the observations I can make, the diagnosis I can make and confirm that there were injuries caused by fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Prosecutor on page 36 now, line I think it was 25 onwards, going on to page 37, you said that when you compiled your report, you did not have the statements and photographs that we discussed. Now, is that necessary to offer you to give your forensic opinion, your medical opinion, about the value of the findings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't need statements or testimony. They are relevant just as a piece of information as to whether one type of weapon was used. So just in that area is the statement important and significant. For example, I mentioned that the witnesses saw skeletonized decomposed body, that was interesting for the decomposition that took place, putrefaction, and that they said they were shot at by the PAM-type weapons, artillery weapons, that there were explosions, that there was shooting from other types of fire-arms. So these fire-arms leave their marks on a body, and I try on the basis of my autopsy findings and observations looking at the corpse to provide evidence to the Court whether that was what happened or not. So if the Court asked me were there injuries caused by explosions, my answer would be yes because on such and such a corpse we found explosive injuries, shells, charring of the body, and so on and so forth, which would be evidence for the Court. But it's not up to me to assess the statement and testimony of individuals; that just serves as a piece of information which I can check out and establish. If I cannot do that, then the witness can think up anything he likes, invent anything he likes, or he might be telling the truth. Everything will depend on the autopsy findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 22, line 10, the Prosecutor put to you a question about ligatures which were associated with the bodies, that was how it read in the original, I don't know what interpretation you received. But could you now tell me, please, how you understood this, the word "associated," did you understand it as the ligatures being tied to the bodies or that the ligatures were in some way linked to the bodies and associated with the bodies in that way?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my interpretation would be that the ligatures were linked to the bodies or found near the bodies or by the bodies, because if you say that somebody was tied then you know what was -- what can be tied, arms, legs, heads, and so on; or they were exhibits attached to the body because they were found next to the body in a given site, somebody might have taken them off the body and sent the body without the ligature. I don't know that, I cannot know that. I understood it as the ligature being connected to the body or linked to the body, just as other things could be linked to the body such as glasses, a cap, a comb, falling out of the clothing the person was wearing, and then all of this is marked and then they say all these objects were found with body number so and so, and this is recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And just one more question linked to Dr. Haglund. Tell me, please, when collective reports are compiled, is the right method from the forensic point of view to include in those collective reports the personal observations of the person compiling such reports, regardless of whether something like that was not observed in the individual autopsy findings? And I am specifically referring to -- well, you were asked a question here on page 21, line 15, that Dr. Haglund in the compilation of these reports relied on photographs and from his own weighing-up of the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, reports can be objective and subjective, but when you compile a collective report from one site, one locality, it has to be highly objective without any subjective elements because then it is no longer conclusions that are made but a subjective opinion of the person compiling it or drafting it. But those opinions must also be based on precisely established facts. So in principle, the subjective point of view must be eliminated as far as possible and the report must be based in objectively established facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And just one more thing that I'd like to ask you and for us to clarify here. In response to my questions and questions from the Prosecutor, you said that you didn't have sufficient time to analyse all the autopsy findings, those up until 2001 as well as those that came in later on and that were conducted by the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, I'd just like to ask you to clarify this point. When you said you didn't have enough time, does that mean that you didn't have enough time because you were too busy with other matters, engaged in other work, or because you didn't have additional time given by us Defence teams because we couldn't provide you with a larger number of working hours?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the latter. I wasn't given more hours, and of course I am very busy doing my own work as a professor and forensic expert. So I was given a certain number of hours, and it was within that number of hours allotted to me that I did the work, although I did -- I put in many more hours of work than the allotted time in order to compile a report that could be useful to this Trial Chamber. So that what the Prosecutor put to me and showed me, the report that I subsequently received and that's why I printed out so that you could see it physically, I need a certain amount of time because it concerns ten bodies. And I read case number 6, for example, for the first time and ad hoc noticed certain points that I would have to explain why I think they should be this way and not the other way. And there are many such reports. I don't know the total number of exhumations and records and photographs, I don't know what the number is up until April 2008. So I could do that within a reasonable space of time allotted to me, and depending on the time given me I will do my best and can compile a report which will be useful to you in order for you to be able to assess what was done later on, from 2002 to 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will be glad to know that we don't have any further questions for you, Professor, and that after three days of solid testimony you will now have the opportunity to return back to your home. However, before you leave this courtroom, on behalf of the Trial Chamber I wish to thank you so much for being so kind to come over and give testimony, which I must say I found extremely, extremely interesting. And on behalf of everyone here present, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the Chamber and everyone else and apologise at the same time if sometimes I went off on a tangent. That's what professors often do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's well-known and that's why it's tolerated here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So documents, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We provided a list, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We have the list here, I don't need to read it out. Mr. Mitchell, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any objections from any of the other Defence teams ? They are all admitted. Mr. Ostojic, I suppose you don't have any documents, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, we do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We have five documents, Your Honour, 65 ter number 3002D.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's the extract that was placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: 65 ter 3474, just the part of Dr. Dunjic's prior statement that I read out; 3485; 3486; and 3487.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Mitchell. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections from any of the other Defence teams? None. So they are also admitted. This brings us to the next witness. Do you wish to make any statements before he is ushered in? Yes, Madam Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. I just wanted to address the Chamber briefly. In the proofing for this witness, with this witness, we received some documentation at the last minute, and I subsequently added them on to our 65 ter list. However, due to the pace of work, we did not formally request that the 65 ter list be expanded. In agreement with the Prosecution colleague who will be examining the witness, she said that she would not object to that. That is why I'm making our request formally in this way, I'm requesting that the list be expanded initially for the documents to be used with the witness and later on tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Ms. Janisiewicz to you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MS. JANISIEWICZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, yes, I do confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to waste time identifying these documents and we can proceed since there is no problem. Meantime, while the witness is being ushered in, Mr. Zivanovic, going through our records we discovered again -- not discovered, realized that we need to crystallise a little bit the situation in regard to what was supposed to be Witness Milka Ilic. It's not clear to us whether you have definitely abandoned the idea of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In which case what we would like you to do is to formally announce while you are standing withdraw her from your 65 ter witness list?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I withdraw her from our Rule 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The other thing, Mr. McCloskey, we received this morning motion tabled by or filed by Ms. Nikolic on behalf of Dragan Nikolic for the addition of two documents to the 65 ter list in relation to the witness who will be coming next week, Professor or Dr. Vuga. If you could possibly give your response to that motion today, if you are in a position to do so; filing which, on Monday which would be the latest, as we need to know what the position is before he starts giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I've seen those, spoken briefly to Ms. Nikolic, and I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we are deciding the motion here and now orally. The motion is granted, amongst other reasons for the fact that it's not being opposed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dobar dan, Gospodine Stojkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you are most welcome as an expert witness produced by or brought forward by Mr. Zivanovic, that being the Defence team for accused Vujadin Popovic in this case. Before you start giving evidence our rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. It's going to be handed to you now by Madam Usher, please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Professor. Please make yourself comfortable. You will first be asked some questions by Mr. Zivanovic who will introduce himself further and he will then be followed by -- my apologies to you, Madam Tapuskovic, also counsel in the Defence team mentioned to you. She will then be followed by others on cross-examination. Madam Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Stojkovic. I have to introduce myself. My name is Mira Tapuskovic, and I am on the Defence team of Mr. Vujadin Popovic. During your testimony I would like to ask you to speak slowly so that everything you say due to the specific terminology that you will be using can be entered in the transcript accurately. First of all, tell us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Oliver Stojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us something about your educational background, please.

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I completed molecular biology, that was my BS; and after that, I had my master thesis and doctoral thesis at the medical school of Belgrade University in the field of molecular genetics.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was your professional clear from the moment you completed your education?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: First I worked at the biological research institute as the research assistants. After that, I worked at the school of biology, Belgrade University, and I was an assistant teacher of molecular genetics. I taught for five years at the school of biology, after which I got employment with the medical school of Belgrade first as a senior research assistant and as of 2006 I am a professor of human genetics at a human genetics chair of the school; and I'm also quite active in the various associations of the Belgrade University.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would have to ask you to speak a bit more slowly since everything needs to be recorded in the transcript. As regards this case, can you remember when you were engaged for the first time by Mr. Popovic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date, but I believe it was in early 2008.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And for this case you drafted a report that you submitted to us?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is Exhibit 1D1069. With the report we also have the expert's CV. Mr. Stojkovic, during your professional career, as you described, in the course of your work, did you cooperate with the International Commission for Missing Persons from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As of 2010 [as interpreted] and until August 2006 I believe I worked as the national coordinator of the DNA programme of the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of work was it? Were you an employee of the ICMP or did that cooperation take part in somewhat different conditions?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was never an ICMP employee --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Janisiewicz.

utterances.speaker: MS. JANISIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, if we could just clarify the dates, they're a bit unclear from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Ms. Tapuskovic, which period of time are you referring the witness to?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember when you started working -- when you started your cooperation with the ICMP from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I might not be able to remember the exact date, but I do believe that it was in 2002 in June I began cooperating with the ICMP. That cooperation was concluded in August 2006. I have to stress again that I cannot recall the exact months. It may have been one or two months before or after that date, but the years are as I stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when you began working with the ICMP, where were you employed and what was your position at the time?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: As I've just tried to explain, I was an employee of the University of Belgrade throughout. First I taught at the school of biology and then at the medical school. In that regard my academic career and my full employment was with the University of Belgrade, and that was never interrupted due to my cooperation with the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us more information about the contents and the framework of your cooperation with the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The ICMP offered to me to sign a letter of appointment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness used the English term.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the exact translation is in B/C/S, as opposed to their regular employees which signed letter of employment. My task with the ICMP had to do with coordinating the DNA programme which was formally the title of my position with the ICMP. The tasks I was assigned had to do with occasional visits to the Sarajevo headquarters. Once a month we held meetings on the topics of DNA programme development as well as development of other ICMP programmes in the region covered by their mandate.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is the region involved?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The ICMP was mandated to operate in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. In that regard they covered the territory of Croatia, Bosnia, Serbia, Kosovo, and Macedonia -- or rather, the territory of the former Yugoslavia where there were armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment, Ms. Tapuskovic, because I think we need to clear this up. There is a bit of confusion here because one -- the witness started off by indicating that he was the national coordinator for this DNA project with ICMP, and then he stated that he was never -- I was never an ICMP employee. Then he mentioned this letter of appointment and it seems that, from what I could see from the transcript, that he used the English term, the same words that I have used. Perhaps he could explain to us whether what was exactly his role and whether he was on the payroll of ICMP while he was conducting this role.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I was -- had just asked that question which wasn't recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the form that your involvement took, your involvement with the ICMP. Did that mean that you changed your employer and were you paid by the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout my involvement with the ICMP, I had not changed my employer at any time, that is to say I was employed at the University of Belgrade throughout. And at that time they were my employer and they still are today, whereas my involvement with the ICMP, International Commission for Missing Persons, was paid by the ICMP itself; and I received remuneration for my work in the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can I interpret that as being just one of the things you did, one of your jobs?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to my involvement with the ICMP, I was also engaged in the commission for the reform of jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice of Serbia, the national commission for security, the Government of Serbia, and many other organizations in which I was active and involved. And I was paid for my involvement on all these projects, in all these institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As we're talking about the ICMP's presence in Serbia, could you tell us in terms of equipment, laboratories, and so on, how did the ICMP function in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The ICMP in Serbia had its offices and their job was to organize the collection of samples, blood samples, from the family and relatives of missing persons and a DNA laboratory, which was housed at the Institute for Forensic Medicine at that time. That's where the laboratory was located. Now, this particular laboratory was a donation from the International Committee for Missing Persons, it was a donation to a Serb organization entitled the Coordination Centre for Kosovo and Metohija. And that laboratory, based on this donors' agreement or contract, although I didn't have an insight into those documents at the time, but anyway it was handed over in 2006 to the Institute for Forensic Medicines for the coordination centre for Kosovo and Metohija so that they could use it all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say laboratory, what does this laboratory incorporate? Does it mean the people working there, the premises, and so on. Tell us what you mean when you say laboratory. What did it comprise of?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The DNA laboratory of the ICMP which was located at the Institute for Forensic Medicine for the Faculty of Medicine of the University of Belgrade incorporated a number of rooms and premises equipped with all the necessary material and equipment for DNA analyses and forensic procedure, and in addition to the premises which were suitable for that type of work, it also had parameters for DNA analysis, it included equipment, state-of-the-art equipment, the most modern equipment in genetics and DNA analysis. And there was one employee working there, working in the laboratory, which was not me.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in the space of the three years that you were involved and working for the ICMP, could you tell us whether you as the coordinator performed any DNA analysis at the request of the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In the DNA laboratory of the ICMP, throughout that period of time, not a single sample was sent in for DNA analysis so that neither I nor my female colleague working in the ICMP ever performed DNA analysis for the requirements of the ICMP or any other analyses for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said no other analysis either, right. Thank you. The Defence teams working on this case and in this trial over the years received many letters, tables, and reports which we provided to you for you to be able to compile your report and which you enumerate in your report. It is 1D1069. Could you please tell us now -- well, the lists of all the documents we sent to you, can you tell us how you checked out the authenticity and validity of the results in the documents provided you.

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence team supplied me with a series of documents in electronic form of which a number of documents related to standard operational procedure in DNA laboratories of the ICMP, standards or SOPs, and the second set of documents were lists with names and other particulars of people who had gone missing and were allegedly identified by means of DNA analyses. In addition to that, I was provided with a number of other documents which were correspondence, for example, between individuals included in this -- these proceedings as well as Dr. Parsons' testimony, who is the active leader of the forensic programme of the ICMP. I studied these in detail, I studied all the documents carefully, all the documents I was sent; and I was not able to find the corresponding parameters in them which would enable me to assess and test the correctness of the findings of the ICMP in respect of the names, matching them up with the names of people on the list that I was provided with.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what the standard elements are of a DNA analysis so that one could test the validity of the analysis?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The SOPs imply, among other things, the name of the laboratory in which the DNA analysis was conducted, the date of the samples, when the samples were taken, the date the analysis was performed, and the date the results were published. Next identificational features for biological trace samples, and in this specific case the skeleton material of the exhumed bodies and identifications and features of the family members of the missing person. And in that the DNA analysis, the DNA analysis would have to include genetic markers which were used in the specific analysis conducted as well as DNA profiles established on the basis of an analysis of the genetic markers from the DNA samples that were analysed. Following that, and finally, in the DNA report you would have to find a verbal description of the conclusion and an opinion stated which must contain biostatistical calculations of the correctness of the assertions made about identity and a conclusion of possibly established identities on the basis of the biostatistical calculations made in that way. You must also have the names of the people that carried out the analysis, and I have to say those are all the elements that are stipulated in the standard operating procedure, the SOP, for considering report on whether DNA matches, DNA matching or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You used the term genetic markers and biostatistical procedure, those two terms. Can you explain them to us more fully. What do you mean by genetic markers?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Genetic markers used in forensic genetics, as that branch of science is called, are defined or were defined as early on as 1994 in the United States of America. After a body that was set up and was called a technical working group for methods of DNA analysis considered which genetic markers of the hundreds of thousands of genetic markers that each person has in his genetic make-up are necessary and should be analysed for each person to be described individually through those genetic markers. Now, this technical working group arrived at a certain number and it was 13 standard genetic markers that they pin-pointed and which are used in the United States of America, and many other countries in the world today, as standard forensic genetic markers for DNA analysis in legal proceedings. Now, as far as biostatistical calculations are concerned, they are calculations based on populational and genetical analysis, the frequency of certain combinations of states with respect to the analysis of genetic markers for a given population for which it is believed that the individual to be identified comes from.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, DNA analyses and to what extent, are they used in order to establish the identity of people in legal cases on the basis of what you were able to see so far?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's absolutely correct. DNA analyses have for a number of years, for about 15 years, are the most important instruments in the hands of the judiciary in order to identify persons who have left biological traces on the site of the crime and that can be linked to a crime committed and are found on the body or in the body of a witness, on the body of the perpetrator of a crime, and so on and so forth. So DNA analysis helps us -- has been helping us over the past two decades and has become a very important instrument in solving criminal cases. In addition to that, DNA analysis is used in courts and in litigation generally in order to establish paternity cases and things of that nature. DNA analysis is also used in humanitarian aims, in the aim of identifying people who were killed in wars or natural disasters; for example, such as the Katrina hurricane disaster or the tsunami in south-east Asia or in wars and conflicts that have occurred in the former Yugoslavia, Iraq, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojkovic. Now may we have on e-court document number 1D1221, and I'd like page 6 of the B/C/S and page 10 of the English to be displayed, please. Mr. Stojkovic, I'm going to read out a portion from the paragraph where you address the Trial Chamber, it's the transcript, the audio recording, from the examination-in-chief of the court in Belgrade on the 22nd of November, 2004, in the case 6/103 or case 6/03. [In English] "I have here results of this electrophoresis in this particular case, and I can give them to the court if need be. So those are the results that are interpreted and cannot be forced later on in the sense that I cannot nor can anyone else make these device to place this pointed parts, spade, on this exact spot.

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Forgeries, falsifications.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojkovic, you said here that you had some electrophoretic analysis that you provided to the Chamber. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Electropherograms represent the results of specific genetic analysis from a specific biological sample analysed at each specific case. It is on the basis of these electropherograms that are collected together and stored in electronic form by the computer which is attached to the system for electrophoresis, and it is on the basis of these electropherograms that the computer with the help of two separate softwares, software programmes, can create, is able to create with the application of certain rules the DNA profile which represents a component part of the DNA report. In the sense that the DNA report that I referred to earlier on and which must necessarily contain the DNA profile can be interpreted independently and autonomously only if with the DNA analysis the electropherogram is supplied as well which shows concrete DNA profiles for a given case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkovic, along with the documents we provided you with, did we also provide you with the electropherograms?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not receive from you a single electropherogram, although I have to mention that I received very little DNA reports as well -- or rather, just three.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you previously explained to us -- well, you used the term biological trace and reference sample. Can you explain what you mean by that, from your point of view, what is a biological trace and what are reference samples?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: According to the definitions of science, biological -- a biological trace is the sample used for DNA analysis whose identity has not yet been established. So this can be, as I said, biological traces found on -- at the crime scene or if we're talking about the results of an identification of a skeleton, biological traces would be parts of the skeletal material, parts of the skeleton. On the other hand, reference samples represent, specifically for DNA analysis, are samples taken most often from the mucous swabs, from saliva, or blood samples taken from the finger or veins from individuals whose identity has been established without doubt in some other way. Reference samples during analysis and professional studies are compared to samples -- or rather, biological traces taken at the crime scene from a given crime. And this kind of comparison is done through the help of biostatistical calculations, on the basis of which the expert will give his opinion as to the identity of the person who could have left a biological trace. And in this type of case the identity of the person to which the skeleton sample belongs.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, must these electropherograms be made for every biological trace and every reference sample?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, before all the courts in Serbia, as well as before all the courts in the United States of America, such electropherograms must be made available to the e-courts themselves and all the parties to a proceeding, that's to say both the prosecution and the defence, so that every side could hire their own respective experts who would then check the trust-worthiness of DNA profiles taken and of the biostatistical calculation taken as well as of the expert opinion given by the expert who had already testified in a given case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we all deserve a break now. 25 minutes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Tapuskovic, you may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkovic, let us resume where we left it off. I have to alert you to the fact that you have to speak slowly so that everything is entered into the transcript. I will continue dwelling on this document, which is 1D1221, we have it on our screens. This is the English version -- or rather, page 10 of the English version, and page 6 of the B/C/S version. This is what the transcript reads: "It is established that Dr. Stojkovic submitted to the court. What is this?" Dr. Oliver Stojkovic, expert witness speaks: "Electropherograms with marked DNA profiles obtained through the analysis of the sent biological samples." Next follows a question by the Presiding Judge: "This can remain in the case files? "Dr. Oliver Stojkovic, expert witness: That is right. It exists in electronic form in my computer and countless originals can be made of it if necessary." Tell us, please, you said there that electropherograms were made and stored in electronic format. Can you tell us what this is like?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Electropherograms are, in fact, electronic documents containing information on all the established signals based on electrophoresis of the then-DNA molecules based on the specific biological trace provided or the specific reference sample provided. This electronic form can be printed out on paper and thus a hard copy can be produced of a specific electropherogram, which can also be used at a later stage to verify the reliability of the analysis carried out. The electronic format itself contains additional information, however, which are not visible in hard copy. For this reason in most of the cases I was asked and submitted to the Court information in electronic form rather than in hard copy. In this specific case I submitted a hard copy because I was not requested to provide them with an electronic copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why it is important to have electropherograms in court proceedings?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The DNA analyses, because they are widely used in court proceedings and because they carry a great probative value in criminal proceedings and litigations alike --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Janisiewicz.

utterances.speaker: MS. JANISIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we're going to object to this line of questioning on relevance grounds. We have no information that that has been requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Tapuskovic, would you like to comment? And in commenting can you indicate the relevance of this line of questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when Witness Parsons was heard, that was on the 1st of February, 2008, he was asked about whether he had brought along electropherograms to present and produce to the Court, his answer was in the negative, that was page 20911. What the significance of electropherograms is, is something that the witness has just been explaining to us. He's been explaining to us what their probative value is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Janisiewicz.

utterances.speaker: MS. JANISIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, our understanding is that they've never asked him to provide - him being the ICMP - to provide electropherograms nor have they ever requested them from us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that correct, Ms. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Your Honour, this was not -- or rather, it -- he was asked that. My further questions will make it clear to you why this line of questioning is important. We want to see in what form electropherograms are made and in what form DNA reports are made, and what it is that the Defence can glean from these electropherograms. The Defence did ask for these electropherograms, but they were denied and I can't recall exactly when this was.

utterances.speaker: MS. JANISIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, we would be interested in more information as to when that request was posed and whether it was posed to the Office of the Prosecutor or to the ICMP directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we can check that at a later stage. I can't give you the information as to when the request was made. I didn't think that this was going to become an issue, but the Prosecution should tell us whether they do have the electropherograms or not. The question put to Mr. Parsons was whether he had submitted electropherograms to the Tribunal, and his answer at that page of the transcript was that he had not submitted electropherograms to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Janisiewicz.

utterances.speaker: MS. JANISIEWICZ
utterances.text: No, I -- we have not requested electropherograms from the ICMP. We in certain instances for certain reasons were provided with some matching reports, but that has not been an issue that we've sought additional material from them on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: MS. JANISIEWICZ
utterances.text: And may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still, if the situation is what has been described, even though the two versions do not exactly tally, why do you still object to the question put by Ms. Tapuskovic asking from the witness, from the expert witness, information as to why electropherograms would be useful?

utterances.speaker: MS. JANISIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, our apologies for not having the exact transcript reference, but our understanding of Mr. Parsons' testimony was that he stated that electropherograms could be used, they are the raw data; however, it's also possible to rely on the established record of the institution and thus --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Stop, stop, because then you're prompting an answer to the witness himself. But let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we've come to the conclusion that the question put by Ms. Tapuskovic is a legitimate one. So, Mr. Stojkovic, if you could answer the question. If you need Ms. Tapuskovic to repeat the question to you, that can be done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the question be repeated, please, but let me tell you something before the question is put to me again. I'd like to say something that might perhaps help to solve the dilemma.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this specific instance of the material that was obtained by the OTP for the Tribunal which had to do with the case in Serbia where I was an expert witness, nobody asked me to produce electropherograms, neither of the parties, because with good laboratory practice and in application of standard operational procedures applied in our country I myself submitted them to the Court in the first place, before anybody had to ask me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to my earlier question, Dr. Stojkovic, and that was: Why is it important to produce electropherograms in court proceedings?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, electropherograms carry high probative value in court proceedings. Sometimes DNA analyses can be overestimated in court proceedings. A specific piece of evidence can be decisive in terms of establishing responsibility for a crime. Electropherogram is the crucial piece of evidence, by the same token as, for instance, a transcript of a given conversation can be proof of the conversation having taken place before the court of law. Failure to produce electropherograms would be tantamount to an expert testifying about a conversation which took place between certain individuals without having had prior insight into the tape of the conversation or the transcript of the conversation. By the same token, a bone sampling can be likened to the tape-recording and -- or to the transcript. Thus, pherograms would indicate the results of the DNA analysis of the bone and the individuals concerned, just as the tape-recording would indicate whether the conversation took place. This is necessary in order for the expert to pronounce his opinion on the reliability of a given piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, without electropherograms, you are not able to advance your opinion about the reliability of a given DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, electropherograms -- that's correct. Electropherograms are one of the elements which I would produce if I were hired by either the Trial Chamber or Prosecution or Defence to testify in respect of some DNA analysis in order to give my opinion as an expert in genetics, I cannot give my expert opinion on specific cases unless I have an insight into electropherograms, just as a physician cannot give his opinion without having an insight into the medical documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, please, Ms. Tapuskovic. Earlier on, page 71, lines 19 and following, you were asked by Ms. Tapuskovic: "Mr. Stojkovic, along with the documents we provided you with, did we also provide you with the electropherograms?" And your answer was: "No, I did not receive from you a single electropherogram, although I have to mention that I received very little DNA reports as well, or rather, just three." Did you ask for more DNA reports and did you ask for electropherograms from the Popovic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't ask for either the reports or electropherograms or any other document given to me by the Prosecution. I merely referred to the documents that were given to me in my report; and since none of them contained anything that I would be able to use in advancing my expert opinion, that was where my engagement for the purposes of the Defence team ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Admittedly, I did state in my report that I would need DNA reports of several cases as well as electropherograms from the same cases in order to be able to draw any sort of an expert conclusion, even at the level of statistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Janisiewicz.

utterances.speaker: MS. JANISIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, in light of the witness's answer, we again question the relevance of this testimony. He has just stated that he did not receive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but he didn't receive them, and he didn't ask --

utterances.speaker: MS. JANISIEWICZ
utterances.text: -- ask for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- for them. Perhaps you can tell Ms. Tapuskovic, and she can relay what you need to say. And at this point it's -- also becomes important for us to know whether indeed a request was tabled with the Prosecution for the provision of these electropherograms or not. That you can tell us or you can confirm at a later stage. Yes, Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you proceeding with the questions on pherograms -- electropherograms or are you moving to something --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more question has to do with electropherograms, that is to say about the way electropherograms are made at the ICMP; and we will answer your query later on because I told you I don't know the date when the request for electropherograms was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's leave this and then move on, Ms. Tapuskovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we call up document, or rather, Exhibit P3235, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkovic -- let's wait for the document to appear. P32 -- I'm sorry 3225. Mr. Stojkovic, do you know what this represents?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is part of the standard operational procedure of the International Commission of Missing Persons called standard operational procedure for the review of DNA matching reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will read one portion in the middle of the paragraph starting with Roman numeral I entitled: "Principle," and I'll read one part of it. [In English] "Match reports contained the following information: Bone sample, code assigned by the submitting pathologist, the bone bar-code assigned at the ICD, a picture of the bone sample including the assigned bar-code, and the measuring device, STR profiles for the bone sample and the potential family reference (often, these are coded for purposes of genetic privacy) ..." [Interpretation] Mr. Stojkovic, coding such reports, is this standard procedure in laboratories dealing with DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, but before I answer that question I wanted to say that all of these elements you mentioned when reading from the principal chapter concerning the contents of a DNA report are the elements I cited as the basic elements of any DNA report. DNA reports need to contain, among others, DNA profiles, which are marked here as STR profiles, but I don't know of any instance of anyone coding those determined DNA profiles in order to protect anyone's genetic privacy.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Even had we been given these reports by the ICMP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Tapuskovic -- Ms. Janisiewicz.

utterances.speaker: MS. JANISIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, if we could ask for the witness to identify one -- the date of the SOP to which he's referring and also to the extent he refers to other standard operating procedures, if he could provide the date and perhaps the file numbers of that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Tapuskovic, you could take care of that with the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the witness to be able to answer the question, could we please go back to page 1 of this document that we have on the screen. Could we please zoom in, and to show us the bottom part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkovic, can you read for us what it says here.

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the first page of this standard operational procedure it says that it was distributed internally DNA, in Sarajevo, the 8th of May, 2007. Also, in my report, I state that on the last page of the report that was forwarded to me there was neither a date nor a signature that would indicate that a specific report was approved. That is why in my report I wrote that the document contains no date and signature, setting aside the internal distribution time that we can see on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: To go back to my previous question then. Had any of the Defence teams asked you to analyse the veracity and authenticity of the individual DNA reports? Irrespective of when those were done, could you have been -- could it have been possible for you to actually ascertain their authenticity because they are coded?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. JANISIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, first -- again, the witness has already testified that he has not asked for electropherograms or DNA reports. To the extent he did have DNA reports in his possession, we would ask that those be identified if referring to any such elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in a position to tell you which reports were handed over to the witness. DNA reports under the following numbers: 1D1242 and 1D1243, and I will get to that one later on while examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think try to condense it because I don't want us to run at a tangent here. The whole issue is the following: Given what you have been given by the Defence team for Mr. Popovic, were you in a position to ascertain the authenticity of the individual DNA reports had you been asked to do that? This is the question basically that it all boils down to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My response to that question is not so simple. It depends on what form of the DNA reports they would be delivered to me. If any of the parties would request me to provide an expert opinion on any such matters, I would first ask to see some 300 DNA reports and the corresponding electropherograms, so as to be able to state anything about their validity. However, if those DNA reports would be delivered to me in electronic form, as stated in the SOP, such DNA reports would then be useless to me for any expertise because -- or rather, except in situations in which I would be also given a key to be able to understand the code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, just stop for a moment, please, Professor. I'd like to seek clearance on this. You were given a bundle of documents relating to DNA analysis by the Defence team for Colonel Popovic; is that correct? Just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What were you asked to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asked to state my position whether, based on the documentation that was at the disposal of the Defence, if it would be possible for me to provide an expert opinion on the authenticity of DNA profiles in the cases pertaining to the Srebrenica event in July 1993 or 1995. It is in the documents. I mentioned that in my report. The request was to offer my comments about the forwarded documents, whether the SOPs I was given in relation to the activities of the ICMP in the process of DNA identification of missing persons are in keeping with the rules of the profession and science. I studied the SOPs in detail and my position was a positive one, save for the SOP pertaining to the publication of a DNA report. I stated that that particular SOP is not transparent and that it makes impossible any additional insight into any additional evidence that may be arriving from the ICMP concerning the identity of the persons involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us move to Exhibit 1D1069. In the English it is page 16. In the B/C/S version it is page 10. Mr. Stojkovic, on the screen in front of you -- well, I can see it's there now. Can you tell me first of all, do you recognise the document?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what it is.

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: That is my report which is an analysis of the documents handed over to me and pursuant to a request made by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3.3 what was your explanation of the issue of coding DNA reports?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This paragraph -- deals with one part of the principles concerning the standard operational procedures dealing with DNA reports studied in which it is stated that specific DNA results are often handed over in coded form. I was of the opinion, as I am now, that it is in complete disaccord with the rules of profession to have any DNA results handed over in coded form. From the text of the SOP principles, it is completely unclear in which cases such coding is done as opposed to in what cases the ICMP chose to hand over to the pathologist involved the original results instead of the coded ones. The frequency of coding is something I could not see from the documents I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the SOP you referred to from the exhibit we just saw, what does the term "genetic privacy" mean?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It is unclear to me what the author of the SOP had in mind when using the term "genetic privacy," given that the genetic markers I have discussed at the beginning of my testimony do not contain any genetic information whatsoever concerning any characteristic of those tested except at the level of matching concerning blood relations between the person whose identity is being sought on the one hand and the persons who gave the samples. The term genetic privacy has to do with the protection of that part of genetic information which have to do with the medically relevant facts on the chances of a certain person to develop specific hereditary diseases or the susceptibility of that person to develop any symptoms of the mentioned hereditary disease or to develop certain behaviour of patterns or any other physiological or pathological symptoms in that person. I also wanted to say again that in the specific forensic genetic analysis, such analysis is not done when analysing specific genetic markers, which as I said were established in 1984; no medical information or any other type of information that needs to be protected cannot be arrived at in analysing these markers. That is why I believe that the argument in favour of genetic privacy, protection, does not stand. On the other hand, it is possible that the author of this SOP had in mind that by coding this information he would be able to protect the genetic information pertaining to the blood relationship between the tested persons. However, even if such information is coded such relationship can be gleaned from other data. Therefore, the argument of genetic privacy, protection, does not stand.

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll read it out. "With reference to your letter, as referenced and dated above, please find enclosed information regarding exhumations and identification carried out in the period from 1996 to 2007 in the area of Srebrenica, including the municipalities of Srebrenica, Bijeljina, Bratunac, Han Pijesak, Kalesija, Kladanj, Rogatica, Sekovici, Vlasenica, and Zvornik. "The information relates to 4.415 identified victims." Now, in preparing for the Defence, Mr. Stojkovic, had you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was shown this document, and I am familiar with its contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're also familiar that we had testimony here from Mr. Parsons, who you mentioned a moment ago -- or rather, I mentioned him a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think I mentioned him too -- but, yes, I am familiar with that. I received from the Defence the transcript of the testimony of Dr. Parsons before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember from the transcript what Mr. Parsons said? When did the ICMP receive accreditation?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that Dr. Parsons said that it was in July of 2007 that the International Commission for Missing Persons received accreditation from a German company for accreditation, which is called DAC.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons spoke about that at 20082, lines 7 to 9 of the transcript. On that page of the transcript, Mr. Parsons said that the accreditation was received in October 2007.

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then I failed to remember that particular piece of information, but I did remember him speaking about it, what the period of time was.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: May we now move on to P2993, page 2, please. May we have page 1 displayed on our screens first, please. Mr. Stojkovic, are you familiar with this document? Was it shown you during preparations for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the contents of this document, and it was shown to me during the preparations.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you read out the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This document is dated the 27th of November, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And whose summary is it, tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Judging by the title page, this summary was compiled by Dean Manning, the former investigator, or rather, former ICTY investigations team leader, the ICTY, Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we can go on to page 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic, I hate to interrupt you, but we've only got one more minute left, basically. So I don't know if you wish to proceed with your questions now. If it's a short question, we can do that; otherwise, we adjourn to Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for that. I would just like to ask one more question to round off this area. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On page 2 here, the lower part of that page, in bold letters it says -- or rather, can you read out what it says.

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: "All victims linked to Srebrenica identified by ICMP by DNA is 5.021."

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stojkovic, my question to you is this: Bearing in mind the date when Mr. Parsons said that the ICMP received its accreditation and bearing in mind the previous letter dated July when the identification of 4.000-odd cases was conducted and this document dated November 2007, if you take all of that into consideration, what is your conclusion, what is the conclusion that follows from all this?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind your previous question with respect to the period of the accreditation itself and all the rest, it is evident that at least 4.000-odd cases which were shown in the previous document were analysed and the identity established before the ICMP had its accreditation for its laboratories and procedures by the accreditation agency.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the 4.451 individuals mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: OLIVER STOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that's the minimum number. So quite possibly of all the 5.021 persons the analysis had been conducted for all of them by October 2007 or November - when was it when the accreditation arrived? - and that the process of identification, DNA analysis, and other procedures as well and comparing data bases, biostatistical calculations, and all the rest of it that is necessary in the SOP, standard operational procedure, which were put to me, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we can break for the day, adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for the week, Ms. Tapuskovic. We'll reconvene Monday morning at 9.00. Thank you. Have a nice weekend everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 30th day of June, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 25
